uncited: Spatial Partitioning for Parallelism divides a volumetric dataset into independent chunks to distribute I/O and computation across multiple processing units, solving the memory and throughput bottlenecks of large-scale volume rendering [1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md][4156-object-space-decomposition-with-local-clustering.md][12593-shardedvolume.md].

It differs from tree-based methods by using fixed or pre-computed spatial divisions rather than hierarchical traversal, and from streaming methods by focusing on static or semi-static data distribution for parallel execution rather than temporal or view-dependent chunk loading [1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md][2369-chunk-based-world-streaming.md].

To prevent boundary artifacts (e.g., black stripes in compositing or discontinuities in isosurfaces) caused by naive non-overlapping division, a small overlap of data may be included among adjacent datasets [1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md].
These extra/duplicated slices are used for boundary calculations but must be removed before final compositing to prevent image stretching [1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md].
The concept of spatial partitioning for parallel volume rendering originated with the need to scale ray-casting and isosurface extraction to datasets exceeding single-node memory.
Early implementations used simple slice-based decomposition across MPI processes [1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md].
Subsequent research introduced graph-partitioning techniques for unstructured grids to minimize communication during rendering [4156-object-space-decomposition-with-local-clustering.md].
More recently, high-level abstractions like ShardedVolume have been developed to manage distributed volumetric data for scientific computing and machine learning workloads [12593-shardedvolume.md].
